query: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloys are promising bond-coat candidates because of their mechanical properties and elevated-temperature oxidation resistance. Earlier HVAF-M3 work identified 15–45 μm feedstock as optimal for high-quality coatings, but applying the same composition and size range with the HVAF-i7 torch yielded acceptable coating quality yet inadequate thickness. Separate studies of conventional MCrAlY bond coats using the M3 system reported a slight gain in deposition efficiency at higher particle velocity and nozzle-specific best spray distances of 300 and 350 mm. The design target is a sufficiently thick, adherent bond coat that retains coating integrity, minimal as-sprayed oxidation, and durability during high-temperature thermal-barrier service, including deposition within internal diameters as small as 120 mm. What single intervention could overcome the thickness limitation? State the hypothesized intervention and mechanism, predict the outcome relative to the 15–45 μm-feedstock baseline, define the deposition and service conditions under which it should remain effective, identify supporting evidence from the cited prior studies, and propose a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Reducing the nozzle-to-substrate distance to approximately 300 mm during HVAF-i7 deposition of FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloy powders (15–45 μm) will increase particle velocity sufficiently to boost the coating thickness by at least 30% relative to the current baseline, while still maintaining minimal in-flight oxidation and robust adhesion.
generation.material_initial_state: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloy powder (15–45 μm size range) with properties previously validated in HVAF-M3 studies.
generation.intervention: Adjust the HVAF-i7 torch parameters to set the spray distance to roughly 300 mm, ensuring that fuel/oxygen flow rates are tuned to preserve an inert atmosphere and maximize particle velocity.
generation.conditions: Deposition under standard HVAF-i7 conditions in an argon-shielded environment. The coatings must perform under service conditions of high-temperature oxidation (up to approximately 900 °C) and adhere even in constrained geometries (internal diameters as small as 120 mm).
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced particle kinetic energy upon impact leads to improved splat flattening and bonding, thereby enabling more effective layer build-up and a denser coating microstructure.
generation.mechanism: By reducing the spray distance, the time particles spend in the high-temperature, oxidizing environment is minimized, which increases their impact velocity and reduces in-flight oxidation. This enhanced kinetic energy promotes better splat formation and intersplat bonding, leading to a thicker, more adherent deposit.
generation.predicted_outcome: The coating thickness will increase by approximately 30% or more compared with deposits made at the current (longer) spray distance, while retaining similar microstructural integrity and oxidation resistance.
generation.baseline: The current HVAF-i7 deposition parameters using 15–45 μm feedstock, which yield acceptable coating quality but insufficient thickness.
generation.boundary: This improvement is expected to hold provided the spray distance is not so short as to cause excessive substrate heating or other thermal damage, and the inert atmosphere is maintained to limit oxidation. The benefits should be observable under standard HVAF-i7 process conditions and service temperatures up to roughly 900 °C.
generation.uncertainty: The exact optimal spray distance for the HVAF-i7 may vary slightly due to system-specific variables. There is also some uncertainty regarding the balance between increased kinetic energy and the potential for increased oxidation or residual stresses.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a controlled experiment in which FeCoNiCrAl coatings are deposited using the HVAF-i7 torch at two different nozzle distances: the baseline distance (greater than 350 mm) and the optimized distance (approximately 300 mm). Ensure that all other deposition parameters (feedstock, fuel/oxygen ratio, substrate preparation) remain constant.
measurements: Coating thickness via cross-sectional scanning electron microscopy (SEM)
In-flight particle velocity measurements using diagnostic tools such as high-speed imaging or laser Doppler velocimetry
Oxidation state assessment by X-ray diffraction (XRD) and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX)
Adhesion strength through standard pull-off tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the optimized spray distance does not produce a statistically significant increase in coating thickness (i.e., less than a 30% increase compared to the baseline) or results in increased oxidation/degradation of adhesion or microstructure compared to the baseline coating, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.kind: web:3.2. Oxidation and Phase Transformations in the Powder during HVOF Spraying
cited_evidence.text: Figure 4 shows the difference in the properties based on the spraying distance. As the spraying distance increases, the average thickness of the coatings slightly decreases due to a stronger scattering of the particles on the longer path. An increase in the spraying distance results in an increase in coating porosity. Porosity depends on the temperature and kinetic energy of the particles []. Particles sprayed from a longer distance have a lower kinetic energy when they strike the substrate, which results in increased porosity. High temperatures and exposure to oxygen lead to the in-flight oxidation of particles; the smaller particles undergo more severe oxidation. With an increase in the spraying distance, the particles are exposed to oxygen for a longer time, which leads to an increased content of oxides (Figure 4d). As the particles oxidize with the formation of alumina, BCC solid solution loses aluminum, which is reflected in a decrease in its lattice parameter (Figure 3b). papers.title: Oxidation Behavior of FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 High-Entropy Alloy Powder.
papers.system: FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 high-entropy alloy powder sprayed via HVOF
papers.approach: The study varied spraying distances (e.g., 150 mm to 250 mm) and observed the effect on in‐flight particle conditions, coating thickness, porosity, and phase evolution
papers.findings: An increase in the spraying distance led to lower particle kinetic energy on impact, resulting in thinner deposits with increased porosity and a higher degree of in‐flight oxidation. The coating properties, such as microhardness, deteriorated with increasing distance due to these effects.
papers.mechanism: Shorter spray distances generate higher particle velocities and less exposure time to oxidation, thereby promoting better splat formation and deposition efficiency; conversely, longer distances allow more oxidation and scattering due to reduced velocity.

papers.title: Comparative Study on the Thermal Performance of Cr-CrₓO_y and YSZ-CoNiCrAlY Coatings Exposed at 900 °C.
papers.system: Conventional MCrAlY bond coats deposited via HVOF/M3 torch
papers.approach: Investigation of deposition parameters, particularly the effect of particle velocity and nozzle-to-substrate distance on deposition efficiency
papers.findings: A slight gain in deposition efficiency was observed with higher particle velocity, with nozzle-specific optimal spray distances around 300 and 350 mm, resulting in improved coating adhesion and performance under high-temperature oxidation conditions.
papers.mechanism: Higher particle velocity increases kinetic energy, promoting a denser, thicker, and well-adhered deposit through enhanced splat formation and reduced in-flight oxidation

established: Higher particle velocities and optimal spray distances are critical in achieving dense and thicker coatings.
In-flight oxidation and scattering of particles are key determinants of coating porosity and thickness.

approaches_tried.approach: Using 15–45 μm feedstock with the HVAF-M3 torch
approaches_tried.outcome: Found to be optimal for achieving high-quality, thick coatings in previous work

approaches_tried.approach: Application of the same feedstock and composition via the HVAF-i7 torch
approaches_tried.outcome: Resulted in acceptable coating quality but an inadequate coating thickness

approaches_tried.approach: Optimizing spray distance in conventional MCrAlY systems (300–350 mm)
approaches_tried.outcome: Slight gains in deposition efficiency and improved adherence were observed

mechanisms: Increasing particle kinetic energy (via reduced spray distance or higher driving pressure) increases momentum upon impact, enhancing splat formation and coating buildup
Reduced dwell time in the high-temperature oxidizing environment minimizes in‐flight oxidation, preserving particle integrity and adhesion
Optimal spray distance balances sufficient particle heating and velocity to ensure melting and densification while limiting oxidation
disagreements: There is some uncertainty about whether feedstock particle size or nozzle distance is the dominant factor—while one study emphasizes particle velocity, another notes that even with optimal feedstock sizes the deposition system (HVAF-i7) does not achieve sufficient build-up.
The degree to which increased particle velocity might also promote unwanted oxidation if the exposure time is not carefully controlled.
open_questions: Can simply reducing the spray distance (or equivalently increasing particle velocity) in the HVAF-i7 setup fully overcome the thickness limitation without introducing deleterious oxidation effects?

How does the altered kinetic energy affect coating integrity, intersplat bonding, and residual stress under service conditions, particularly within confined geometries (e.g., internal diameters as small as 120 mm)?
What is the interplay between feedstock size, spray distance, and deposition system design (HVAF-i7 vs. HVAF-M3) in governing the final coating thickness?
opportunities: Combine the optimal feedstock size (15–45 μm) with an optimized spray distance (targeting 300–350 mm) in the HVAF-i7 system to enhance particle kinetic energy, thereby improving deposition efficiency and coating thickness
Investigate adjusting operational parameters (fuel/oxygen ratio, nozzle design) in the HVAF-i7 torch to more closely replicate the higher particle velocities obtained in the M3 setup
Conduct systematic experiments that vary only the nozzle stand-off distance in the HVAF-i7 system while maintaining constant feedstock to isolate the effect of increased velocity on coating buildup
Examine performance under high-temperature oxidation and in confined deposition environments (e.g., 120 mm internal diameters) to validate service durability

directions.direction: Optimize nozzle‐stand‐off distance to boost particle velocity and deposition efficiency.
directions.assessment: This approach directly increases the kinetic energy of the particles, which improves splat formation and intersplat bonding. Evidence from conventional MCrAlY studies cites optimal spray distances (300–350 mm) that improved deposition efficiency (see query background and PMC10820071::web::010). This intervention is directly related to the thickness limitation and is experimentally feasible with the HVAF-i7 system.

directions.direction: Adjust fuel/oxygen ratios to elevate flame temperature and drive higher particle speeds.
directions.assessment: Modifying the combustion parameters could similarly boost particle kinetic energy. However, this route might increase in-flight oxidation if not balanced properly and is less directly supported than the spray distance explanation.

directions.direction: Preheat the substrate to enhance splat flattening and coating adhesion.
directions.assessment: This could improve bond coat adhesion and promote thicker builds by enhancing in-flight splat solidification. Yet, it may also risk increased oxidation and thermal stress, making it a less direct solution for the thickness limitation.

directions.direction: Refine the feedstock particle size distribution or morphology.
directions.assessment: While feedstock characteristics are important and a 15–45 μm range has been optimal with the HVAF-M3 system, the current evidence indicates that the issue with HVAF-i7 is more linked to processing parameters (specifically, particle velocity), so altering the feedstock is less likely to overcome the thickness limitation.

directions.direction: Introduce an auxiliary in-flight heating phase (pre-heating) to enhance particle melting before impact.
directions.assessment: This concept could, in theory, improve melting and deposition efficiency; however, it adds complexity to the process and increases the risk of oxidation. Its mechanism is less directly supported by prior studies compared to nozzle distance optimization.

choice.direction: Optimize nozzle‐stand‐off distance to boost particle velocity and deposition efficiency
choice.why: Because adjusting the spray distance directly increases particle kinetic energy—thereby enhancing splat formation and deposit build-up—and is supported by conventional MCrAlY studies that show optimal performance at 300–350 mm (see query background and PMC10820071::web::010). This intervention is straightforward to implement on the HVAF-i7 system without changing the feedstock composition.
